title: Linear systems you will actually use
hook: Two batteries side by side feed one lamp, each through its own internal resistance. Both currents are unknown, and each one changes the other. How do you find the current each battery gives?
oneBreath: A fact like x + y = 7 about two unknown numbers has a whole line of possible answers, and a second fact gives a second line, so the one pair that fits both is where the two lines cross. You can find that pair exactly, either by swapping one rule into the other or by adding the rules so a letter drops out, and you can tell when there is no single answer. Then you turn two facts from a story, or the rules for currents at a junction and voltages round a loop, into two equations and solve them.

ideas.title: Where two lines meet
ideas.oneLine: The pair of numbers that makes two equations true at once is the point where their two straight lines cross on a graph.

ideas.title: Substitution
ideas.oneLine: When one equation says what y equals, swap that into the other equation, which leaves one unknown to solve, then find y from it.

ideas.title: Elimination
ideas.oneLine: Add or take away the two equations, after scaling one or both if needed, so that one unknown cancels out and one unknown is left.

ideas.title: From words to two equations
ideas.oneLine: Two separate facts about the same two unknowns, such as two receipts or two readings from a machine, give two equations you can solve.

ideas.title: Kirchhoff's laws: two loops
ideas.oneLine: Kirchhoff's junction law for currents and loop law for voltages turn a two-loop circuit into two equations in two unknown currents.

ideas.title: Three unknowns (stretch)
ideas.oneLine: Removing the same letter from two different pairs of three equations leaves two equations in two unknowns, which elimination already solves.

calibration.q: One rule says y is double x, plus 1. Another says y is double x, plus 5. Which x and y fit both rules?
calibration.why: For any x, the second rule's y is 4 more than the first's, so no pair fits both: their lines are parallel. x = 0 and y = 1 fits only the first rule, and x = 2 and y = 1 just copies numbers off the rule.

calibration.q: a + b = 9 and a − b = 3 are both true. Add the two left sides together and the two right sides together. What do you get?
calibration.why: a + a is 2a, b take away b is nothing, and 9 + 3 is 12, so 2a = 12, giving a = 6. 2a + 2b = 12 loses the minus on the second b, and 2a = 6 takes the right sides away instead of adding them.
